power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: This study developed a data-driven decision-support framework to project annual hospital admissions and in-hospital mortality for ischemic heart disease (IHD) and cerebrovascular disease in Suriname from 2023 through 2050.Using retrospective discharge data from 2013-2022 across three major public hospitalsaccounting for approximately 71.8% of national admissions-historical trends were analyzed using log-linear regression across six age groups.
text.formatted: This study developed a data-driven decision-support framework to project annual hospital admissions and in-hospital mortality for ischemic heart disease (IHD) and cerebrovascular disease in Suriname from <ref type="formula">2023 through 2050.</ref>Using retrospective discharge data from 2013-2022 across three major public hospitalsaccounting for approximately 71.8% of national admissions-historical trends were analyzed using log-linear regression across six age groups.

text.text: Population projections relied on the UN World Population Prospects 2024 Revision.

Future admissions and deaths were modelled across five policy pathways: status quo, current HEARTS, strengthened HEARTS, full HEARTS targets, and full HEARTS combined with improved hospital survival, with uncertainty assessed via 10,000 Monte Carlo simulations.
Results showed that admission rates increased for most age groups between 2013 and 2022.
Under the status quo pathway, combined cardiovascular admissions are projected to reach 15,592 in 2030, 30,772 in 2040, and 62,643 in 2050.

Compared to the status quo in 2050, projected admissions would drop to 58,073 under current HEARTS, 41,690 under strengthened HEARTS, and 27,469 under full HEARTS-representing median reductions of 6.0%, 33.5%, and 56.1%, respectively.
Additionally, projected 2050 deaths would decrease from 2,644 under the status quo to 1,155 under full HEARTS, and further to 924 with improved hospital survival.
Cardiovascular hospital demand could rise substantially if historical trends continue, impacting health-system capacity.

While not causal estimates or precise forecasts, these modelled pathways illustrate how routine health data can create a transparent framework to guide cardiovascular prevention, resource allocation, and health-system planning in Suriname.
Cardiovascular disease remains one of the major public health challenges facing countries throughout the Region of the Americas(1) .

Its consequences extend beyond premature mortality and morbidity to increasing demands on health services, including emergency care, inpatient services, diagnostic capacity, medicines, specialist care and rehabilitation (2) .
text.formatted: Its consequences extend beyond premature mortality and morbidity to increasing demands on health services, including emergency care, inpatient services, diagnostic capacity, medicines, specialist care and rehabilitation <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(2)</ref> .

text.text: These pressures are particularly important in health systems where financial; workforce and infrastructure constraints limit the ability to expand services in response to rapidly increasing demand (2).
text.formatted: These pressures are particularly important in health systems where financial; workforce and infrastructure constraints limit the ability to expand services in response to rapidly increasing demand <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(2)</ref>.

text.text: Ischemic heart disease (IHD) and cerebrovascular disease are major contributors to cardiovascular morbidity and mortality.
Both are strongly associated with modifiable risk factors, particularly hypertension, diabetes, tobacco use, obesity and physical inactivity.
Hypertension is especially important because it contributes to both IHD and cerebrovascular disease and can be addressed through population-level prevention and strengthened primary care (3) .
text.formatted: Hypertension is especially important because it contributes to both IHD and cerebrovascular disease and can be addressed through population-level prevention and strengthened primary care <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(3)</ref> .

text.text: For health-system decision-makers, however, documenting current disease burden is only one part of the policy problem.
Historical surveillance describes what has happened, but does not directly indicate how hospital demand may evolve under different future policy trajectories.

A health system therefore needs evidence not only about the magnitude and direction of current disease trends, but also about the potential consequences of alternative choices regarding prevention, primary care and hospital services (4).
text.formatted: A health system therefore needs evidence not only about the magnitude and direction of current disease trends, but also about the potential consequences of alternative choices regarding prevention, primary care and hospital services <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(4)</ref>.

text.text: Suriname provides an important setting in which to examine this issue.
Previous analyses of hospital discharge data from the country's major public hospitals demonstrated sustained increases in cardiovascular and renal disease burden between 2013 and 2022 (5) .
text.formatted: Previous analyses of hospital discharge data from the country's major public hospitals demonstrated sustained increases in cardiovascular and renal disease burden between 2013 and 2022 <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5)</ref> .

text.text: The observed increase in cardiovascular hospital utilization occurred in parallel with persistent exposure to cardiovascular risk factors and continuing demands on a health system with limited specialist and hospital capacity (6).
text.formatted: The observed increase in cardiovascular hospital utilization occurred in parallel with persistent exposure to cardiovascular risk factors and continuing demands on a health system with limited specialist and hospital capacity <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(6)</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, Suriname has begun strengthening cardiovascular prevention through the HEARTS initiative (2) .
text.formatted: At the same time, Suriname has begun strengthening cardiovascular prevention through the HEARTS initiative <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(2)</ref> .

text.text: HEARTS in the Americas promotes standardized cardiovascular risk management, evidence-based hypertension treatment, access to essential medicines and technologies, team-based care, and systematic monitoring (7) (8) (9) .
text.formatted: HEARTS in the Americas promotes standardized cardiovascular risk management, evidence-based hypertension treatment, access to essential medicines and technologies, team-based care, and systematic monitoring <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(8)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(9)</ref> .

text.text: The Surinamese implementation program has expanded substantially, but early implementation data have also identified challenges related to continuity of care, workforce capacity, infrastructure, medicines and financing.

The implementation study documented 56 participating facilities, 460 healthcare workers and 11,187 patients, while 52.6% of patients had at least one follow-up visit and bloodpressure control among patients with follow-up measurements reached 56.2% (10).
text.formatted: The implementation study documented 56 participating facilities, 460 healthcare workers and 11,187 patients, while 52.6% of patients had at least one follow-up visit and bloodpressure control among patients with follow-up measurements reached 56.2% <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(10)</ref>.

text.text: These developments create a policy-relevant question: how might future cardiovascular hospital demand differ if current trends continue compared with alternative trajectories involving progressively stronger cardiovascular prevention and improved hospital care?
Scenario modelling can provide one approach to answering this question.

By combining routinely collected hospital data, population projections and program implementation parameters, epidemiological evidence can be translated into alternative future trajectories that can be compared at relevant planning horizons.

The objective of this study was therefore to develop a data-driven decision-support framework to project annual IHD and cerebrovascular disease hospital admissions and in-hospital mortality in Suriname from 2023 through 2050.
We additionally examined alternative policy pathways representing progressively stronger cardiovascular prevention through HEARTS and improved hospital survival.

The projections for 2030, 2040 and 2050 were selected as decision horizons to illustrate the potential implications of alternative policy trajectories for long-term health-system planning and resource allocation.
We conducted a retrospective hospital-based time-series study followed by model-based projections of IHD and cerebrovascular disease hospital admissions and in-hospital mortality.
The historical analysis used annual hospital discharge data from three major public hospitals in Suriname covering 1 January 2013 through 31 December 2022.
These hospitals collectively accounted for approximately 71.8% of all hospital admissions in Suriname during the study period.
The 71.8% figure represents overall hospital activity and should not be interpreted as diseasespecific national coverage.
Acute IHD is predominantly managed at the major hospitals receiving patients with acute cardiovascular presentations.
Cerebrovascular disease admissions are concentrated at the largest referral hospital, although additional patients are admitted to other private hospitals.

The participating hospitals therefore provide a substantial and clinically relevant source of hospital data for modelling cardiovascular hospital demand, but the dataset does not constitute a complete national registry of all IHD or cerebrovascular disease events.
Hospital admissions were identified from discharge diagnoses recorded in the hospital databases.
IHD was defined using ICD-10 codes I20-I25.
Cerebrovascular disease was defined using ICD-10 codes I60-I69, consistent with the disease definitions used in the preceding analyses of the research program.

Because the I60-I69 category includes I69, which represents sequelae of cerebrovascular disease, the operational outcome is referred to as cerebrovascular disease rather than stroke throughout this manuscript.
The analysis used six age groups: 0-29, 30-39, 40-49, 50-59, 60-69, and ≥70 years.
The unit of analysis was the hospital admission, rather than the individual patient.
Patients with multiple admissions during the study period could therefore contribute more than one observation.
Unique patients were not identified or deduplicated.
Transfers between participating hospitals could also have been recorded as separate admissions and may therefore have resulted in double counting of a single clinical episode.
Discharge status was available for all but 28 admissions.
These 28 admissions with unknown discharge diagnosis were excluded from further analysis.
Accordingly, the analysis represents recorded hospital admissions with an available discharge status rather than unique patients or incident disease events.
The projection model was developed as a decision-support framework rather than as a conventional predictive forecasting model.

The framework linked three components [1] observed historical hospital admission trends; [2] projected population change; and [3] alternative assumptions regarding cardiovascular prevention and hospital survival.
text.formatted: The framework linked three components <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> observed historical hospital admission trends; <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> projected population change; and <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> alternative assumptions regarding cardiovascular prevention and hospital survival.

text.text: The purpose was to translate routinely collected epidemiological data into alternative future trajectories that could be compared at clinically and operationally relevant planning horizons.
The primary outputs were annual hospital admissions and in-hospital deaths.
Results were summarized for 2030, 2040 and 2050 because these years represent near-, medium-and longterm planning horizons.
The framework was intended to support policy deliberation rather than determine a single optimal policy.
It does not incorporate intervention costs, budget constraints, cost-effectiveness, workforce feasibility or competing health priorities.

For each age group (a) and disease (d), annual admission rates from 2013-2022 were modelled using log-linear regression: ln 𝑅 (𝑎,𝑑,𝑡) = 𝛽 0(𝑎,𝑑) + 𝛽 1(𝑎,𝑑) (𝑡) where R a,d,t denotes the annual admission rate for age group a, disease d, and year t.

The estimated coefficient for calendar year was converted to an annual percentage change (APC) using the formula APC = (𝑒 𝛽 1 -1) × 100 with corresponding 95% CIs derived from the standard error of the estimated regression coefficient.
All annual observations available within the historical period were used for estimation.
The resulting APC estimates represented the annual multiplicative change in admission rates under the fitted log-linear model.
Population estimates for 2023-2050 were derived using annual population growth rates projected by the United Nations Population Division.
The annual rates were obtained from the United Nations World Population Prospects 2024 Revision (11).
text.formatted: The annual rates were obtained from the United Nations World Population Prospects 2024 Revision <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(11)</ref>.

text.text: The projected annual population growth rate declined from 0.909% in 2023 to 0.264% in 2050.
The annual rates were applied sequentially to the population estimates to derive annual population values through 2050.
Because the UN annual population growth rates used in the analysis were not age-specific, the same annual growth rate was applied to each of the six age groups in each projection year.

The resulting age-specific population values therefore represent model-derived estimates based on UN-projected annual population growth rather than directly extracted age-specific UN population projections.
For each age group and disease, annual hospital admissions were projected sequentially from the 2022 baseline.

The final implementation of the model applied the estimated annual diseasespecific admission trend together with the annual population growth rate: 𝐴 (𝑎,𝑑,𝑡) = 𝐴 (𝑎,𝑑,𝑡-1) * (1 + 𝐴𝑃𝐶 (𝑎,𝑑) (1 + 𝑔 𝑡) , where A (a,d,t) is the number of admissions in age group a, disease d, and year t; APC (a,d) is the estimated annual percentage change; and g t is the UN-projected annual population growth rate.
The age-and disease-specific estimates were summed to obtain total annual hospital demand.
All projected values represent conditional trajectories under specified model assumptions, rather than predictions of the exact future number of admissions.
For the primary status quo projection, age-and disease-specific case-fatality rates (CFRs) observed in 2022 were held constant throughout the projection period.
Projected deaths were calculated as: 𝐷𝑒𝑎𝑡ℎ𝑠 (𝑎,𝑑,𝑡) = 𝐴𝑑𝑚𝑖𝑠𝑠𝑖𝑜𝑛𝑠 (𝑎,𝑑,𝑡) × 𝐶𝐹𝑅 (𝑎,𝑑,2022)
This provided a transparent baseline in which future changes in hospital survival were not assumed unless explicitly incorporated into a scenario.

Because the COVID-19 pandemic may have affected hospital utilization, admission patterns, and outcomes during 2020-2022, its potential influence on the long-term trend estimates was assessed separately through a COVID-exclusion sensitivity analysis.
Five policy-relevant pathways were modelled.
Historical admission trends and projected population growth continued without an additional HEARTS-related effect.
Age-and disease-specific CFRs remained at 2022 levels.
This pathway represented the current level of HEARTS implementation.
It assumed [1] 80% program reach; [2] 52.6% treatment/follow-up retention; and [3] 56.2% blood-pressure control among patients retained in follow-up.
text.formatted: It assumed <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> 80% program reach; <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> 52.6% treatment/follow-up retention; and <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> 56.2% blood-pressure control among patients retained in follow-up.

text.text: These assumptions resulted in modelled reductions in admissions of 7.5% for IHD and 10.8% for cerebrovascular disease.
The 80% program reach was a modelling assumption, not an observed estimate of national HEARTS coverage.
The 52.6% followup and 56.2% control estimates were derived from available implementation data (10).
text.formatted: The 52.6% followup and 56.2% control estimates were derived from available implementation data <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(10)</ref>.

text.text: Because reporting was incomplete across participating facilities, they were not interpreted as nationally representative population estimates.
This pathway retained 80% program reach and 56.2% blood-pressure control while increasing treatment/follow-up retention to 80%.
The resulting modelled reduction in admissions was 35.6% for both IHD and cerebrovascular disease.
This pathway assumed [1] 80% program reach; [2] 80% treatment/follow-up retention; and [3] achievement of the predefined HEARTS target for blood-pressure control.
text.formatted: This pathway assumed <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> 80% program reach; <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> 80% treatment/follow-up retention; and <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> achievement of the predefined HEARTS target for blood-pressure control.

text.text: The resulting modelled reduction in admissions was 58.9% for both IHD and cerebrovascular disease.
This pathway retained the admission reductions of Pathway 4 and additionally applied a 20% reduction in age-and disease-specific CFRs.
The 20% CFR reduction was treated as an illustrative modelling assumption, not an empirically established effect of HEARTS or improved hospital care in Suriname.
The pathways therefore represent counterfactual policy trajectories, not causal estimates of intervention effectiveness.

The relationship between population hypertension control and cardiovascular mortality was parameterized using the ecological analysis by Martinez and colleagues, which examined 36 countries in the Americas (12).
text.formatted: The relationship between population hypertension control and cardiovascular mortality was parameterized using the ecological analysis by Martinez and colleagues, which examined 36 countries in the Americas <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(12)</ref>.

text.text: The study reported associations between population hypertension control and mortality from IHD and stroke.
The reported associations were not specific to Suriname, HEARTS, hospital admissions, or in-hospital mortality.

Accordingly, the external estimates were used as model parameters within a counterfactual scenario framework rather than interpreted as direct causal estimates of the effect of HEARTS on hospital admissions.

The OWSA identified several age-and disease-specific trends that strongly influenced projected outcomes.

In the internal temporal holdout assessment, models fitted to 2013-2019 and used to estimate 2020-2022 demonstrated strong correspondence between observed and model-estimated values.
Across the 36 age-disease-year combinations, the correlation was r=0.964, with R²=0.889, MAE of 117.5, RMSE of 179.7, and MAPE of 20.18%.
The MAPE was 20.43% for IHD and 19.92% for cerebrovascular disease.
These results support the usefulness of the trend framework for scenario analysis while also demonstrating meaningful prediction error.
The temporal assessment therefore does not establish precise long-term predictive accuracy.
Excluding the COVID-19 period from trend estimation had a limited effect on the long-term trajectory.

The deterministic 2050 projection increased from approximately 56,959 admissions under the primary specification to approximately 57,643 admissions when the 2020-2022 period was excluded, corresponding to a difference of approximately 1.2%.

The findings suggest that the long-term status quo trajectory was not primarily driven by the inclusion of the pandemic years.
This study demonstrates how routinely collected hospital data can be transformed into a quantitative framework for cardiovascular health-system planning.
Three findings are particularly important.
First, if historical admission trends continue, Suriname could experience a substantial increase in annual cardiovascular hospital demand.
The status quo pathway projected 62,643 annual IHD and cerebrovascular disease admissions by 2050, with a 95% UI of 46,351-102,113.
Second, alternative prevention pathways produced substantially different trajectories.
By 2050, projected admissions were approximately 6% lower under current HEARTS, 34% lower under strengthened HEARTS and 56% lower under the full HEARTS pathway.
Third, prevention and hospital care address different components of the health-system problem.
Prevention primarily changes the number of cardiovascular events reaching hospital, whereas improved hospital survival changes the probability of death among patients who are hospitalized.
The combined pathway therefore generated the lowest projected mortality (14) .

A central contribution of this study is to demonstrate how routinely collected hospital data can be transformed into actionable evidence for public-health policy and health-system planning(4) .

In settings such as Suriname, where comprehensive population-based disease registries may be limited, routinely generated hospital information can nevertheless provide an important basis for identifying emerging patterns in cardiovascular disease and anticipating future service needs.

By combining observed age-and disease-specific admission trends with population projections and alternative prevention and cardiovascular-care scenarios, this study moves beyond describing historical burden to examining how different policy pathways could shape future hospital demand (15) .

text.text: For health systems with constrained resources, preventing avoidable cardiovascular events can therefore be viewed simultaneously as a public-health objective and a capacity-management strategy.

The findings support a healthsystem approach in which investments in primary prevention, hypertension detection and control, treatment continuity, and cardiovascular risk management are considered alongside investments in emergency and inpatient care.

Such integration is consistent with the broader objective of strengthening health systems by reducing preventable demand while ensuring that adequate capacity remains available for patients who develop acute cardiovascular disease (20).

In particular, the assumed 80% reach represents a policy scenario rather than observed national coverage.
The value of the analysis is instead that it makes implementation ambition measurable in terms of potential downstream demand.

The policy implication is consequently not that every age-specific projection should be treated as certain, but that prevention strategies should include younger and middle-aged adults rather than relying primarily on interventions delivered after cardiovascular risk has already accumulated.

This is particularly relevant to health-system strengthening because prevention initiated earlier in the life course may reduce future demand while simultaneously improving population health (25, 27, 28).

Increasing cardiovascular demand may place pressure on emergency departments, diagnostic imaging, cardiology and neurology services, interventional procedures, inpatient nursing, rehabilitation, medicines, and post-discharge follow-up (29) .

text.text: Importantly, the findings do not imply that prevention can substitute for investment in acute cardiovascular services.
Even under the most effective modelled prevention pathway, substantial cardiovascular demand remains.
Rather, prevention can reduce avoidable demand while health systems maintain sufficient capacity for patients who continue to experience acute events (30) .

text.text: The results may therefore assist health authorities in considering where additional investments are likely to have the greatest long-term system value, including hypertension control, continuity of chronic care, emergency cardiovascular pathways, diagnostic capacity, specialist workforce, and rehabilitation.

Because the underlying data cover three major public hospitals and approximately 71.8% of overall hospital admissions during the study period, the projected absolute numbers should not be interpreted as a complete national estimate of service requirements.
Their principal value for policy is to demonstrate the potential direction and relative scale of future demand and the extent to which alternative prevention pathways could modify it.

The widening differences between scenarios over time have an important implication for publichealth policy: decisions made during the current decade may influence the health-system pressures experienced decades later.
The divergence between the status quo and higherimplementation scenarios was already evident by 2030 and became substantially larger by 2040 and 2050.

This temporal pattern is relevant because strengthening primary care, improving hypertension control, developing the cardiovascular workforce, and expanding hospital capacity all require time to implement.
Delaying action until demand reaches its projected maximum may therefore constrain the ability of the health system to respond efficiently.
At the same time, the projections should not be interpreted as certainty about the level of demand in 2050.

The temporal holdout analysis demonstrated good agreement between observed and predicted admission patterns but also meaningful prediction error, and the probabilistic analysis showed increasing uncertainty over longer projection horizons.

The most appropriate policy use of these findings is therefore not to plan a fixed system around a single 2050 estimate, but to use 2030, 2040, and 2050 as planning horizons and reassess trajectories as new data become available.
This supports a proactive rather than reactive approach to cardiovascular health-system strengthening.
The uncertainty surrounding long-term cardiovascular demand further supports an adaptive approach to health-system planning.

In the present analysis, uncertainty increased substantially toward 2050, and the one-way sensitivity analysis identified specific age-and disease-specific trends that contributed disproportionately to variation in projected outcomes.

For example, the trend for cerebrovascular disease among adults aged 30-39 years produced the largest relative range for projected admissions, while cerebrovascular trends in several other age groups also contributed substantially to uncertainty.
These findings have practical implications for surveillance priorities: improving the quality and completeness of age-specific cardiovascular data could directly strengthen future planning.

Rather than treating the projections as a one-time forecasting exercise, health authorities could use the framework as part of an iterative planning cycle in which hospital trends, hypertension-control indicators, HEARTS implementation, and health-system capacity are periodically reassessed and projections updated.
Such an approach is consistent with a learning health-system model in which routine data are continuously converted into information for policy adaptation (31, 32) .

text.text: The value of the framework therefore lies not in eliminating uncertainty, but in making uncertainty explicit, identifying the parameters that matter most, and creating a mechanism through which improved surveillance and program implementation can progressively improve future decision-making.
This study has several strengths that enhance its relevance for public-health policy and healthsystem planning.

First, it uses a decade of routinely collected hospital data and disaggregates cardiovascular admission trends by disease and age group, allowing heterogeneous trajectories to be identified rather than assuming a uniform cardiovascular trend.
Second, the framework integrates observed hospital trends with projected population growth and explicitly defined prevention and cardiovascular-care pathways.
Third, the analysis links epidemiological projections to a real-world health-system intervention, HEARTS, while clearly distinguishing observed program indicators from modelling assumptions.

Fourth, uncertainty was examined using both probabilistic sensitivity analysis and one-way sensitivity analysis, allowing the overall uncertainty of the projections and the parameters most influential to outcomes to be identified.

Fifth, temporal holdout assessment provided an internal assessment of model performance against more recent observed admission patterns, while exclusion of the COVID-19 period assessed the influence of pandemic-related disruption on the long-term trend estimates.
Finally, the framework is transparent enough to be updated as new routine health data and program indicators become available.

This combination of routine surveillance, scenario modelling, and implementationoriented interpretation provides a potentially transferable approach for other health systems in the Americas where data are incomplete but policy decisions nevertheless require forward-looking evidence.
Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings.
First, the analysis was based on hospital discharge data from three major public hospitals and therefore does not constitute a complete national population-based registry.

Although these hospitals represented approximately 71.8% of overall hospital admissions during the study period, disease-specific coverage may differ, particularly because cardiovascular admissions also occur in private hospitals.

Second, the unit of analysis was the hospital admission rather than the unique patient; individuals with multiple admissions could therefore contribute more than once, and transfers between participating hospitals may result in more than one admission being recorded for a single clinical episode.
Third, disease classification was based on discharge diagnoses and may be influenced by diagnostic and coding practices.

Fourth, the historical trend model assumes that past age-and disease-specific trends provide an informative basis for long-term extrapolation, although future epidemiological, demographic, treatment, and health-system conditions may differ from those observed during 2013-2022.
Fifth, the population projections were derived from UN-projected annual population growth rates and applied sequentially across age groups because age-specific annual growth rates were not used.
Sixth, the status quo mortality scenario assumes that 2022 age-and disease-specific case-fatality rates remain constant throughout the projection period.

Seventh, the HEARTS scenarios combine observed program indicators with assumptions about future program reach, treatment/follow-up retention, and blood-pressure control; incomplete program reporting means that these indicators should not be interpreted as nationally representative estimates.
Eighth, the assumed 80% program reach and the 20% case-fatality reduction in Scenario 5 are illustrative modelling assumptions rather than empirically established national effects.

Ninth, the external hypertension-control associations were derived from an ecological study across countries in the Americas and were not specific to Suriname, HEARTS implementation, or hospital admissions.

Finally, the PSA captures uncertainty in the stochastic parameters included in the model but does not encompass all forms of structural uncertainty, including future changes in disease incidence, treatment patterns, hospital utilization, program implementation, coding practices, or unforeseen health-system shocks.
The projections should therefore be interpreted as scenario-based decision-support estimates rather than precise predictions of national cardiovascular admissions or deaths.
Suriname may face a substantial increase in cardiovascular hospital demand if the admission trends observed between 2013 and 2022 continue.
Under the status quo pathway, combined annual IHD and cerebrovascular disease admissions were projected to reach 62,643 by 2050, with a 95% uncertainty interval of 46,351-102,113.
The modelled policy pathways demonstrated that progressively stronger cardiovascular prevention could substantially alter this trajectory.
Under the full HEARTS pathway, projected 2050 admissions were approximately 56% lower than under status quo.
An additional illustrative improvement in hospital survival further reduced projected deaths without changing the admission trajectory.
These findings should not be interpreted as precise forecasts or causal estimates of HEARTS effectiveness.
Their principal value lies in demonstrating how routinely collected health data can be transformed into a transparent, policyrelevant decision-support framework.

For Suriname, the findings support an integrated approach in which sustained investment in hypertension control and cardiovascular prevention is combined with continued strengthening of acute cardiovascular and cerebrovascular care.

More broadly, the study illustrates how health systems with limited resources can use routine epidemiological data not only to describe current disease burden, but also to explore alternative futures and inform decisions about prevention, capacity, workforce, medicines, surveillance and resource allocation.
Suriname's future cardiovascular hospital burden is therefore not predetermined.
The trajectory will depend in part on the policy choices, implementation capacity and health-system investments made today.

S4 and S5trajectories overlap exactly for admissions because scenario S5 affects in-hospital mortality only, not admission demand (see Figure3).

The figure demonstrates that without intervention, Suriname faces substantial growth in cardiovascular hospital demand; full HEARTS implementation could reduce 2050 admissions by approximately 56% relative to status quo.

Figure 2: Projected annual cerebrovascular disease hospital admissions in Suriname, 2023-2050Deterministic projections of annual hospital admissions for cerebrovascular disease (ICD-10: I60-I69; predominantly acute ischemic stroke and intracerebral haemorrhage) in Suriname from 2023 through 2050, under identical scenario definitions as Figure1.

Cerebrovascular disease shows steeper projected growth under the status quo scenario (S1) compared to ischemic heart disease, driven by higher age-specific annual percentage change (APC) coefficients in younger age groups, particularly ages 30-39 years (cerebrovascular APC: 12.73% vs ischemic heart disease APC: 9.25%).
This age-pattern sensitivity is captured in the one-way sensitivity analysis presented in supplementary materials.

As with Figure1, scenarios S2-S4 progressively reduce admission volume through improved cardiovascular risk factor management and treatment adherence, while S5 applies the same admission trajectory as S4 with an additional 20% reduction in casefatality rates to model improved hospital-based acute stroke care.
Vertical reference lines indicate planning milestones(2030, 2040, 2050).
S4 and S5 admissions overlap completely; mortality benefits of S5 are shown separately in Figure3.
Full HEARTS implementation (S4) could reduce 2050 cerebrovascular admissions by approximately 57% relative to status quo.

The comparison between Figures1 and 2illustrates how diseasespecific APC heterogeneity affects long-term projections and underscores the importance of age-stratified modelling for health-system planning.
Figure 3: Projected annual in-hospital deaths in Suriname, 2023-2050 Two-panel deterministic projections of annual in-hospital deaths from cardiovascular disease in Suriname from 2023 through 2050.
Panel A shows deaths from ischemic heart disease (ICD-10: I20-I25); Panel B shows deaths from cerebrovascular disease (ICD-10: I60-I69).
All scenarios (S1-S5) are based on applying age-and disease-specific case-fatality rates (CFR) derived from 2022 hospital discharge data.
For scenarios S1-S4, case-fatality rates are held constant throughout the projection period, allowing isolation of mortality burden attributable to changes in admission volume alone.

Scenario S5 applies the same admission trajectory as S4 (identical to Figures1 and 2) but incorporates an additional 20% relative reduction in ageand disease-specific CFR, representing an illustrative estimate of potential mortality gains from improved in-hospital acute care, post-acute management, and secondary prevention (e.g., thrombolysis, thrombectomy, intensive care protocols, discharge planning).

This scenario is purely illustrative and not empirically grounded in observed data; it is included to demonstrate the complementary role of hospitallevel survival improvements alongside population-level admission prevention.
Under the status quo (S1), inhospital deaths from both conditions more than double by 2050.
S4 (full HEARTS) reduces 2050 deaths by approximately 56% for both diseases through admission prevention alone.

S5 provides an additional 20% mortality reduction via CFR improvement, illustrating a potential pathway to more than 60% combined mortality reduction by 2050 if both prevention and acute-care quality are simultaneously advanced.
Vertical reference lines denote planning milestones(2030, 2040, 2050).
The divergence between S4 and S5 in Panel A and B is most pronounced at later projection years, reflecting the cumulative effect of the CFR reduction applied to large absolute numbers of admissions.
The status quo pathway demonstrated substantial growth in annual cardiovascular hospital demand over the projection period.
Combined annual IHD and cerebrovascular disease admissions were projected at 15,592 in 2030; 30,772 in 2040; and 62,643 in 2050.
The probabilistic 2050 status quo estimate was 62,643 admissions (95% UI 46,351-102,113).
The increasing uncertainty at longer projection horizons reflects the compounding effect of uncertainty in the underlying ageand disease-specific temporal trends.

The projections therefore indicate that continued historical trends could create a substantial increase in cardiovascular hospital demand, even without assuming further deterioration in population health.
